# Accuracy at full data, and robustness {#sec-full-data}

With the full training split of either dataset, MeshTransformer2 (MT2)
and GeoTransolver reach the same accuracy on high-lift wings and
GeoTransolver is 1.085x more accurate on cars; what separates the two
architectures at full data is not accuracy but behaviour off the tuned
operating point. MT2 holds its accuracy across a decade of learning rate
where GeoTransolver degrades 4--14x, and is exactly covariant to rigid
motions without any frame estimation. Sampling-density robustness
depends on the configuration: MT2 with the similarity gauge loses 1.20x
under a 10:1 sampling bias where GeoTransolver loses 3.6x, but the
constant-gauge configuration behind every accuracy number in this book
loses 13--14.5x, and the gauge costs 8% at 35 training cases. Pose
covariance is a contract rather than an accuracy edge on vehicle data,
and exact query independence, the property that would make MT2 a true
evaluate-anywhere surrogate, is an optional configuration that costs
3.0--3.7x in accuracy; the reference configuration behind every result
in this book does not have it. Peak training memory at 10,000 tokens is
9.8 GB for MT2 as trained, 3.6 GB with the exact pool-then-project
rewrite, against 4.6 GB for GeoTransolver.

This chapter is the full-data counterpart of the data-efficiency result
in @sec-data-efficiency, where the two architectures separate by 2.5--2.8x
at 35--210 training cases. Here they do not separate, and the chapter's
job is to say precisely how they do not, and what else is true of each at
that operating point.

## The verdict in one paragraph {#sec-program-review}

At full data the two architectures are at parity on HiLiftAeroML and MT2
is 8.5% behind on DrivAerML (@sec-full-data-accuracy), so in-distribution
accuracy at industrial scale does not separate them. Where they differ
is off the tuned operating point: MT2 is robust to learning rate
(@sec-robustness-lr) and exactly pose-covariant (@sec-pose-contract),
while its density robustness holds only with the similarity gauge on
(@sec-robustness-density) and its exact query independence is an
optional configuration bought with accuracy (@sec-query-independence).
The resources behind every comparison are in @sec-cost, and the
DrivAerML measurements are collected on one instrument in @tbl-frontier.

## In-distribution accuracy at full data {#sec-full-data-accuracy}

**At each architecture's best learning rate, MT2 and GeoTransolver are at
parity on HiLiftAeroML (0.041 vs 0.042) and MT2 is 1.085x behind on
DrivAerML (0.0577 vs 0.0532).** The metric throughout is the relative L2
error of surface pressure as defined in @sec-metrics: the recipe's
relative L2 on the standardized pressure field over the sampled points
of a case, measure-weighted, arithmetic mean over the validation cases.
The HiLift number is on the shared 180-case validation set of the
curated full split (1,260 training cases); the DrivAerML number is on
the 48-car validation split of the 435-car training set (@sec-splits).
Both are seed means over seeds 42 and 43, evaluated at the final epoch
of the frozen protocol of @sec-protocol (10,000 sampled surface points
per case, 500 epochs, bf16, no augmentation); no checkpoint was selected
on validation error.

The best learning rate was chosen per architecture by validation on the
full split, from the grid of the next section, before any other
experiment in this book used it: 1e-3 for MT2 on both datasets, 1e-3 for
GeoTransolver on HiLift and 3e-3 for GeoTransolver on DrivAerML. The
DrivAerML gap does not depend on that choice: at MT2's own rate of 1e-3
GeoTransolver scores 0.0548 (0.0546/0.0550) against MT2's 0.0577, 1.05x
ahead, and best-vs-best it is 1.085x ahead (0.0532 at 3e-3 against
0.0577).

The HiLift parity holds case by case, not only on average. Scoring each
of the 180 validation cases by each architecture's two-seed mean error
gives 180 case-level pairs; MT2 has the lower pressure error in 130 of
them, and in 103 it is lower on both seeds separately. The median
GeoTransolver/MT2 ratio is 1.06 with an interdecile range of 0.92--1.18,
and the exact sign test on n = 180 rejects equality (p = 2e-9), so MT2
is nominally ahead, but the per-case advantage is a few percent, far
smaller than the roughly threefold median ratio at 35 training cases
(@sec-de-paired).^[`results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07.json`,
key `1260`.] In force coefficients on the
same 180 cases (mean absolute error relative to the mean absolute
coefficient), MT2 predicts drag to 1.4% and lift to 0.9%, GeoTransolver
to 1.2% and 0.8%. Both are at the level where the two are
interchangeable for an engineering user.

The comparison is fair by the criteria of @sec-fair-comparison: matched
tokens per case and epochs, each architecture at its own best learning
rate, shared validation cases, and a matched parameter count (MT2 8.9M
against GeoTransolver 9.0M). Memory was not matched: the MT2
checkpoints were trained at 9.8 GB peak against GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB.
The exact pool-then-project rewrite computes the same function at
3.6 GB (fp64 maximum difference 4e-15; @sec-cost), so the extra memory
bought no accuracy, but no MT2 result in this book was produced at or
below GeoTransolver's footprint. The comparison is also narrow: two
seeds, one validation split per dataset, and no test-split evaluation of
the full-split models (the sealed test splits are spent on regime
extrapolation, @sec-regime-extrapolation).

## Learning-rate robustness {#sec-robustness-lr}

**Across the learning-rate grid MT2's worst point is within 1.55x of its
best on DrivAerML and 1.14x on HiLiftAeroML, while GeoTransolver
degrades 4--14x at 1e-2 on DrivAerML and 3.5--9.4x at 3e-3 on HiLift.**
The grid is {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2} on DrivAerML and {1e-3, 3e-3} on HiLift,
two seeds (42, 43) per cell except the DrivAerML 3e-3 cell, which holds
the three GeoTransolver seeds (42--44) and five MT2 seeds (42--46) of the
frozen-protocol training runs; every other setting is held at the frozen
protocol. The quantity in @fig-lr-robustness is the validation pressure
rel-L2 defined above; a point is one seed and the line joins seed means.

On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver at 1e-2 scores 0.739 and 0.221 on its two
seeds against its best of 0.0532, a degradation of 13.9x and 4.1x that
also differs by 3.3x between seeds. MT2 at 1e-2 scores 0.0874 and 0.0914
against its best of 0.0577, a degradation of 1.55x on the seed mean with
the two seeds within 5% of each other. On HiLift the same pattern appears
one step lower on the grid: GeoTransolver at 3e-3 destabilizes to 0.397
and 0.148 (9.4x and 3.5x its best of 0.042) where MT2 scores 0.045 and
0.049 (1.14x its best of 0.041 on the seed mean), and across the whole
HiLift grid MT2's four results lie in 0.040--0.049 while GeoTransolver's
lie in 0.041--0.397. The robust architecture is the one whose worst grid
point is within a factor of two of its best; only MT2 satisfies that on
either dataset.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lr-robustness
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Learning-rate robustness at full data. Validation pressure rel-L2
#|   (log scale) against learning rate for GeoTransolver (red circles)
#|   and MeshTransformer2 (blue squares); small markers are individual
#|   seeds (42 and 43 in every cell except DrivAerML 3e-3, which holds
#|   GeoTransolver seeds 42--44 and MT2 seeds 42--46), lines join seed
#|   means. Left: DrivAerML, 435
#|   training cars, 48 validation cars. Right: HiLiftAeroML full split,
#|   1,260 training cases, the shared 180-case validation set. Protocol:
#|   10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bf16, no
#|   augmentation. How to read it: the vertical spread of one colour
#|   across the grid is that architecture's sensitivity to learning rate.
#|   It does not show seed sensitivity at a fixed rate, which is a
#|   different property and is larger for MT2 (@sec-shared-floor), and
#|   it does not show any rate below 1e-3. Data:
#|   results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json (DrivAerML 1e-3,
#|   1e-2), results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/round3_reduction.json,
#|   mt2_v3c_reduction.json and mega_reduction.json (DrivAerML 3e-3),
#|   results/highlift_wave_reduction.json (HiLift).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

RES = Path("..") / "results"
SW = RES / "mixedres_training_2026-07-31" / "sweep"
iw = json.load(open(RES / "instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json"))
round3 = json.load(open(SW / "round3_reduction.json"))
mt2_const = json.load(open(SW / "mt2_v3c_reduction.json"))  # MT2, constant gauge, lr 3e-3
mega = json.load(open(SW / "mega_reduction.json"))
hl = json.load(open(RES / "highlift_wave_reduction.json"))

# DrivAerML grid: per-seed pressure rel-L2 at each learning rate
dr = {"gt": {}, "mt2": {}}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    for lr_key, lr in (("lr1e3", 1e-3), ("lr1e2", 1e-2)):
        dr[arch][lr] = [iw[f"iw_{arch}_{lr_key}_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
dr["gt"][3e-3] = [round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["sweep_metrics"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
dr["mt2"][3e-3] = ([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
                   + [mega[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (45, 46)])
# HiLift full split: per-seed pressure rel-L2 at 1e-3 and 3e-3
hlg = {"gt": {}, "mt2": {}}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    hlg[arch][1e-3] = [hl[f"{arch}_hl_lr1_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
    hlg[arch][3e-3] = [hl[f"{arch}_hl_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]

style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o"), "mt2": (BLUE, "MeshTransformer2", "s")}
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 4.6), sharey=True)
for ax, grid, title in zip(
        axs, (dr, hlg),
        ("DrivAerML (435 train / 48 val cars)", "HiLiftAeroML full split (1,260 train / 180 val)")):
    for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
        c, name, mk = style[arch]
        lrs = sorted(grid[arch])
        means = [statistics.mean(grid[arch][lr]) for lr in lrs]
        ax.plot(lrs, means, color=c, lw=2.0, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
        for lr in lrs:
            ax.scatter([lr] * len(grid[arch][lr]), grid[arch][lr], color=c, s=16, alpha=0.9, zorder=4)
        # Direct labels at the midpoint of the last segment: GeoTransolver's steep
        # segment leaves room to its upper left, MT2's flat segment to its lower side.
        xm = (lrs[-2] * lrs[-1]) ** 0.5
        ym = (means[-2] * means[-1]) ** 0.5
        txt = f"{name}\nworst/best = {max(means) / min(means):.2f}x"
        if arch == "gt":
            ax.annotate(txt, (xm, ym), xytext=(-10, 6), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                        fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", ha="right", va="bottom",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
        elif ax is axs[0]:
            ax.annotate(txt, (xm, ym), xytext=(6, -10), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                        fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", ha="left", va="top",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
        else:
            ax.annotate(txt, (xm, ym), xytext=(0, -12), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                        fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="top",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks(sorted(grid["gt"]))
    ax.set_xticklabels([f"{lr:g}" for lr in sorted(grid["gt"])])
    ax.set_xlim(6e-4, 1.6e-2)
    ax.set_xlabel("Learning rate [–]", color=INK2)
    ax.set_title(title, color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10.5, pad=8)
    ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
axs[0].set_yticks([0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8])
axs[0].set_yticklabels(["0.03", "0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40", "0.80"])
axs[0].set_ylim(0.026, 1.0)
axs[0].set_ylabel("Validation pressure error, rel-L2 [–]  (log)", color=INK2)
fig.suptitle("Learning-rate robustness at full data (points: seeds; lines: seed means)",
             x=0.02, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.94))
plt.show()
```

The consequence for practice is that MT2 can be trained at a
protocol-default learning rate on a new dataset without a sweep, while
GeoTransolver's best rate must be found per dataset (it differs between
the two datasets here) and a rate one step too high can cost a factor of
ten. The scope is two seeds per cell (three to five in the DrivAerML
3e-3 cell) and two datasets; the grid does not
extend below 1e-3, and nothing here says where either architecture's
instability begins on other datasets. Robustness to learning rate and
robustness to seed are different properties: MT2 has the larger
seed-to-seed prediction spread on both datasets (@sec-shared-floor).

## Sampling-density robustness {#sec-robustness-density}

**Under a 10:1 spatially biased sampling density, MT2 with the similarity
gauge degrades 1.20x, GeoTransolver 3.6x, the exact-kernel
MeshTransformer (MT1) about 1.8x (1.6--2.2x across three seeds), and MT2
with the constant gauge 13--14.5x.** The 1.20x figure belongs to a
configuration that produced no accuracy number in this book; every
accuracy result uses the constant gauge, which is the 13--14.5x row. The
probe evaluates a trained DrivAerML model on the 48
validation cars with surface points drawn ten times more densely in one
region of the car than elsewhere, with exact Horvitz--Thompson measure
weights so that any weighted integral is unbiased; the readout is the
ratio of the pressure rel-L2 under the biased sampling to the same
model's rel-L2 under uniform sampling at 10,000 points. A ratio of 1.0
means the prediction depends only on the surface and not on how it was
sampled.

The gauge is the pair of reference quantities MT2 uses to make its
invariant inputs dimensionless: the centroid from which positions are
measured and the reference length that scales them (@sec-mt2). With the
constant gauge the centroid is an unweighted mean of the sampled points,
which moves by 0.94 RMS radii under the 10:1 bias, and every downstream
invariant moves with it. With the similarity gauge both the centroid and
the reference length are measure-weighted (the RMS radius of the
surface), so a biased sample estimates the same gauge as a uniform one.

| architecture | uniform 10k pressure rel-L2 | 10:1 biased pressure rel-L2 | degradation ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| MT2, similarity gauge (seeds 42 / 43) | 0.0638 / 0.0629 | 0.0766 / 0.0758 | 1.20x / 1.20x |
| MT2, constant gauge (seeds 42 / 43) | 0.0636 / 0.0627 | 0.926 / 0.812 | 14.5x / 13.0x |
| GeoTransolver (seed 42) | 0.0530 | 0.192 | 3.6x |
| exact-kernel MT1 (seeds 42 / 43 / 44) | 0.141 / 0.134 / 0.145 | 0.235 / 0.298 / 0.238 | 1.7x / 2.2x / 1.6x |

: Sampling-density robustness on DrivAerML. Columns: validation pressure
rel-L2 (48 cars) with 10,000 uniformly sampled points; the same with a
10:1 spatially biased sampling and exact measure weights; and their
ratio (biased / uniform; 1.0 means sampling-independent predictions).
All models are trained on the 435-car split under the frozen protocol at
learning rate 3e-3; the two MT2 rows differ only in the gauge setting
and are seed-matched. Data:
results/s1_similarity_gauge_2026-09-03.json (MT2 rows);
results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/round3_reduction.json
(uniform column) and p3v3_reduction.json (biased column) for
GeoTransolver and MT1. {#tbl-density}

What the gauge costs depends on the data budget. At full DrivAerML data
it is neutral in-family: 0.0638/0.0629 against 0.0636/0.0627 on pressure
with the same seeds, and the same on wall shear. At 35 HiLift training
cases it costs 8% (0.149 against 0.138 in the single-factor ablation of
@sec-mechanism), which is why no accuracy result in this book uses it.
It also does nothing for zero-shot transfer to a held-out vehicle family, which
stays at mean-predictor level with or without it (@sec-limits), so
absolute geometric size was not what limited cross-family transfer. MT1's
intermediate robustness is what its intrinsic gauge and measure contract
buy (@sec-mt1); GeoTransolver's 3.6x is the cost of geometry-adaptive
statistics computed from the sample rather than from the surface. The
scope is one probe geometry (one bias pattern at one ratio) on one
dataset, and the GeoTransolver figure is a single seed.

## Pose: a contract, not an accuracy edge {#sec-pose-contract}

**MT2 is exactly covariant to rotations and translations, and
GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at
1.01x accuracy cost; on vehicle data, equivariance is therefore a
contract rather than an in-distribution accuracy advantage.** The
readout is the ratio of validation pressure rel-L2 under random SO(3)
poses of every validation car to the same model's rel-L2 in the
dataset's native pose. MT2's ratio is 1.00 by construction, verified in
fp64 (@sec-mt2). GeoTransolver trained in the native frame degrades
26--32x across three seeds. GeoTransolver trained with the
canonicalization of @sec-pose (freestream to +x, roll fixed from the
geometry's principal axes) scores 0.0536/0.0535 in-pose and
0.0536/0.0534 on the random-pose orbit, against 0.0530/0.0533 for the
native-frame model in its native pose: exactly pose-invariant, 1.01x
behind. Closing the same hole by rotation augmentation instead costs
GeoTransolver 1.87x in-family (@tbl-frontier).

What MT2's contract still buys is generality: it needs no known freestream
direction and no sign-resolvable principal frame, both of which
canonicalization requires and both of which every vehicle case here
supplies (0 of 48 validation cars has a degenerate frame). Where those
conditions fail, on a geometry with a degenerate inertia tensor or in a
setting without a global flow direction, the canonicalized model has no
frame to compute and the equivariant one is unaffected. That is the
whole of the claim; there is no accuracy dividend to add to it.

## Query independence and its price {#sec-query-independence}

**In its reference configuration MT2's prediction at a surface point
depends weakly on which other points were sampled with it, about 7%
against 2% for GeoTransolver; the optional query-independent
configuration removes that dependence exactly, at a 3.0--3.7x cost in
accuracy.** Query independence means that the prediction at one surface
point does not depend on which other points are in the same forward
pass. Neither architecture has it as trained here. In MT2's reference
configuration, which is the one behind every HiLift and DrivAerML
surface result in this book, the output heads read directly from the
interacting encoder tokens, so every sampled point is simultaneously an
input that shapes the slices and a query that reads them, and redrawing
the companions of a point changes its prediction. The readout is
companion-set sensitivity: hold a shared prefix of 5,000 cells fixed,
redraw the rest of the 10,000-point sample, and measure the relative
change of the predictions on the prefix. It is about 7% for MT2 and 2%
for GeoTransolver, which sees the whole sample the same way and is
simply less sensitive to it.

The query-independent configuration of MT2 (@sec-mt2) replaces the
readout with passive read blocks: queries read the slice and boundary
tokens and never write to them, so a point evaluated alone gives the
same answer, to fp64 roundoff, as the same point in a batch of 10,000.
It has 11.0M parameters against the reference configuration's 8.9M. Its
price on DrivAerML pressure is measured two ways. Passive decode of every
surface point scores 0.203--0.211 against the reference configuration's
0.0577 at the same learning rate of 1e-3, 3.5--3.7x. An
anchor-conditioned variant, in which a fixed core of 2,560 interacting
tokens carries all the interaction and every surface point decodes
passively from it, scores 0.209/0.221 against 0.0697/0.0671 for the
reference configuration trained at 6,500 tokens per case, 3.0--3.3x seed
by seed; the two runs have matched peak training memory (6.35 GB against
6.56 GB, both in the as-trained implementation of @sec-cost), which is
what makes the 6,500-token run the right comparator. Across the two
measurements the cost lies between 3.0x and 3.7x. The token-count
control is itself informative: the reference configuration at 6,500
tokens is 8% worse than at 10,000 (0.0684 against 0.0633 at the same
learning rate), so the query-independent design lost 3x to a control
that had already given up 8%.

The consequence is a choice, not a defect: a surrogate in this family
can have exact evaluate-anywhere semantics at about three times the
error, or GeoTransolver-class accuracy with a few percent of sensitivity
to how the boundary was sampled. It cannot at present have both. The
interior task, where off-surface queries are always decoded passively,
prices the same trade at 2.6x from the other direction (@sec-interior).

## Cost {#sec-cost}

**At 10,000 tokens per case MT2's peak training memory is 9.8 GB as
trained and 3.6 GB with the exact pool-then-project rewrite, against
GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB; MT2's forward plus backward step takes 283 ms.**
The MT2 figures are measured under bf16 autocast on an RTX 4090 with
hidden width 192, 12 layers, 256 slices and batch 1; the GeoTransolver
figure is the peak of its training run on the same protocol, which
includes optimizer state (under 0.2 GB for a 9M-parameter model). The
relational readback can be computed either as project-then-pool, which
materializes a per-point-per-slice activation in every layer and peaks
at 9.8 GB, or as pool-then-project, an exact identity since the routing
weights sum to one (@sec-mt2-cost), which peaks at 3.6 GB. Every MT2
checkpoint in this book was trained with the former, at 2.1x
GeoTransolver's memory. The two implementations agree to 4e-15 in fp64
with the same parameters, so the extra memory bought no accuracy; but
no MT2 run in this book was carried out at or below GeoTransolver's
footprint, and the 3.6 GB figure is a property of the rewrite, not of
the reported results. No matched step-time figure for GeoTransolver on
the same instrument is among the artifacts, so only memory is compared
across architectures here.

## The frontier in one table {#sec-review-frontier}

@tbl-frontier collects the DrivAerML measurements of this chapter on one
instrument. Every row is trained on the 435-car DrivAerML split at
learning rate 3e-3 (the frozen rate, common to all rows; MT2's
best-vs-best figure at its own rate is in @sec-full-data-accuracy),
500 epochs, 10,000 tokens per case, and scored on the 48 validation cars.
The columns are:

- **In-family (x GeoTransolver)**: validation pressure rel-L2 at 10,000
  uniformly sampled points, divided by the GeoTransolver reference row's
  value; 1.00 is GeoTransolver's accuracy, larger is worse.
- **Zero-shot (fastback)**: mean normalized pressure L2 on the DrivAer
  fastback family (@sec-shift-suv), which no row trained on: the
  single-family rows trained on DrivAerML alone, the two-family rows on
  DrivAerML plus the estate family. Scoring every row on the same
  held-out family is what makes the column comparable down its length.
  A value of 1.0 is the level of predicting the mean.
- **Density (10:1)**: the degradation ratio of @tbl-density, biased over
  uniform sampling.
- **Pose (random SO(3))**: the degradation ratio of @sec-pose-contract,
  random poses over native pose; 1.00 is exact invariance.
- **Peak memory**: peak training memory at 10,000 tokens per case as
  trained; for the MT2 rows the figure with the exact pool-then-project
  rewrite follows in parentheses (@sec-cost).

```{python}
#| label: frontier-table
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path

RES = Path("..") / "results"
SW = RES / "mixedres_training_2026-07-31" / "sweep"
mega = json.load(open(SW / "mega_reduction.json"))
round3 = json.load(open(SW / "round3_reduction.json"))
mt2_const = json.load(open(SW / "mt2_v3c_reduction.json"))  # MT2, constant gauge, lr 3e-3
probe = json.load(open(SW / "probe_reduction.json"))
p3v3 = json.load(open(SW / "p3v3_reduction.json"))
s1 = json.load(open(RES / "s1_similarity_gauge_2026-09-03.json"))["runs"]
p1pp = json.load(open(RES / "p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json"))["results"]

def mean(vals):
    return sum(vals) / len(vals)

# GeoTransolver reference: in-family pressure rel-L2 and zero-shot fastback, seeds 42-44
gt10_seeds = {s: round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["sweep_metrics"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)}
gt10 = mean(list(gt10_seeds.values()))
gt_zs = mean([round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["smoke_fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
# pose: random-SO(3) pressure rel-L2 over native-pose rel-L2, per seed
gt_pose = [probe["p1_rot"][f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["mean"] / gt10_seeds[s] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
mt2_pose = (mt2_const["mt2_v3c_seed42"]["p1_rot"]["mean"]
            / mt2_const["mt2_v3c_seed42"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"])
rot_pose = mega["gt_rotaug_seed42"]["p1_rot"]["mean"] / mega["gt_rotaug_seed42"]["in10k"]["mean"]
# density: biased over uniform (GeoTransolver seed 42 on the same instrument as the MT2 rows)
gt_dens = p3v3["gt_fixed_seed42"]["mean"] / gt10_seeds[42]
mt2_dens_const = [s1[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["p3_ratio_vs_infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
mt2_dens_gauge = [s1[f"iw_mt2_gauge_seed{s}"]["p3_ratio_vs_infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]

rot_in = mean([mega[f"gt_rotaug_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])
rot_zs = mean([mega[f"gt_rotaug_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])
canon_in = mean([p1pp[f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["inpose_raw"][0] for s in (42, 43)])

mt2c_in = mean([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
               + [mega[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (45, 46)])
mt2c_zs = mean([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["smoke_fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
gauge_in = mean([s1[f"iw_mt2_gauge_seed{s}"]["infamily"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])
gauge_zs = mean([s1[f"iw_mt2_gauge_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])

mt2m_in = mean([mega[f"mt2_multi_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
mt2m_zs = mean([mega[f"mt2_multi_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
gtm_in = mean([mega[f"gt_multi_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
gtm_zs = mean([mega[f"gt_multi_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])

GT_MEM, MT2_MEM = "4.6 GB", "9.8 GB (3.6 GB)"
rows = [
    ("GeoTransolver (9.0M), native frame", 1.0, gt_zs, f"{gt_dens:.1f}x",
     f"{min(gt_pose):.0f}--{max(gt_pose):.0f}x", GT_MEM),
    ("GeoTransolver + rotation augmentation", rot_in / gt10, rot_zs, "not measured",
     f"{rot_pose:.2f}", GT_MEM),
    ("GeoTransolver, canonical frame", canon_in / gt10, None, "not measured",
     "1.00 (canonicalized)", GT_MEM),
    ("MT2 (8.9M), constant gauge", mt2c_in / gt10, mt2c_zs,
     f"{min(mt2_dens_const):.1f}--{max(mt2_dens_const):.1f}x", f"{mt2_pose:.2f} (exact)", MT2_MEM),
    ("MT2 (8.9M), similarity gauge", gauge_in / gt10, gauge_zs,
     f"{mean(mt2_dens_gauge):.2f}x", "1.00 (exact)", MT2_MEM),
    ("GeoTransolver, two families", gtm_in / gt10, gtm_zs, "not measured", "not measured", GT_MEM),
    ("MT2, two families, constant gauge", mt2m_in / gt10, mt2m_zs, "not measured", "1.00 (exact)", MT2_MEM),
]
out = ("| configuration | in-family (x GeoTransolver) | zero-shot (fastback) | density (10:1) "
       "| pose (random SO(3)) | peak memory |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n")
for (n, i, z, d, r_, m) in rows:
    zs = f"{z:.2f}" if z is not None else "not measured"
    out += f"| {n} | {i:.2f}x | {zs} | {d} | {r_} | {m} |\n"
print(out)
print(f": The DrivAerML frontier at full data. In-family: validation pressure "
      f"rel-L2 at 10,000 uniformly sampled points on 48 cars, relative to the "
      f"GeoTransolver native-frame reference ({gt10:.4f}, seeds 42--44); all "
      f"rows at learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs, bf16. Zero-shot (fastback): "
      f"mean normalized pressure L2 on the DrivAer fastback family, which no "
      f"row trained on (single-family rows train on DrivAerML alone; "
      f"two-family rows on DrivAerML plus the estate family); 1.0 is the "
      f"level of predicting the mean. Density (10:1): pressure rel-L2 under "
      f"10:1 spatially biased sampling with exact measure weights, over the "
      f"same model's rel-L2 under uniform sampling (GeoTransolver seed 42; MT2 "
      f"seeds 42/43). Pose: pressure rel-L2 under random SO(3) poses over "
      f"native-pose rel-L2 (GeoTransolver seeds 42--44; augmentation and MT2 "
      f"seed 42; MT2's covariance is exact by construction and verified in "
      f"fp64, so its ratio is 1.00 for every checkpoint). Peak memory: "
      f"training memory at 10,000 tokens per case as trained (MT2 with the "
      f"relational readback computed as project-then-pool; GeoTransolver from "
      f"its training run); in parentheses, the same MT2 model with the exact "
      f"pool-then-project rewrite (@sec-cost). Seeds per cell: GeoTransolver "
      f"reference 3, augmentation 2, canonical frame 2, MT2 constant gauge 5 "
      f"in-family and 3 zero-shot, MT2 similarity gauge 2, two-family rows 3. "
      f"Data: "
      f"results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/{{mega,round3,mt2_v3c,probe,p3v3}}_reduction.json, "
      f"results/s1_similarity_gauge_2026-09-03.json, "
      f"results/p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json. {{#tbl-frontier}}")
```

Three things to read off the table. First, at the common learning rate
MT2 is 1.20x behind GeoTransolver in-family; at each architecture's best
rate the gap is 1.085x (@sec-full-data-accuracy), and the table's
column is the conservative one for MT2. Second, on the common held-out
fastback family no single-family row transfers: GeoTransolver scores
0.59 (0.82 with rotation augmentation) and MT2 0.95--0.99 in either
gauge, against 1.0 for predicting the mean, and neither gauge nor pose
handling moves this; a second training family moves both architectures
to 0.11--0.13. Cross-family transfer is a property of training-data
diversity, not of anything in the architecture column (@sec-limits),
although GeoTransolver's single-family failure is the milder one. Third,
the two robustness columns are where the rows differ by more than a seed
spread: MT2 with the similarity gauge is the only configuration that is
both sampling-robust and pose-robust without a frame estimate. At full
DrivAerML data it pays nothing for this in the in-family column
(0.0638/0.0629 against 0.0636/0.0627 for the constant gauge), but at 35
HiLift cases the gauge costs 8% (@sec-robustness-density), and it is not
the configuration behind any accuracy number in this book; the memory
column is the same for every MT2 row.

## What is shared and what is not at full data {#sec-shared-floor}

**At full data, 70% of each architecture's residual is shared with the
other on identical points, seed disagreement no longer predicts error,
and accuracy is still rising with tokens per case; the current
understanding is that both architectures approach a common floor set by
the protocol at this token count.** The measurements behind that
sentence are three.

The shared residual. Two GeoTransolver and two MT2 full-split
checkpoints (the learning-rate 3e-3 pairs on DrivAerML, the 1e-3 pairs
on HiLift) were evaluated on bit-identical validation points (10,000 per
case) and their four pressure residual fields were averaged point by
point; the shared fraction of a case is the measure-weighted energy of
that mean residual divided by the mean of the four models' residual
energies, so it is 1.0 when the four residuals coincide and 0.25 when
they are mutually orthogonal with equal norms. Averaged over cases it is
0.71 on DrivAerML (48 cars) and 0.70 on HiLift (180
cases).^[`results/n1_noise_floor_2026-09-01.json`, `shared_residual_fraction`.]
Whatever the two architectures get wrong at full data, they
mostly get wrong together, and equally so on the two datasets. This is
a measured fact about the residuals and nothing more; the probe cannot
separate shared inductive bias from any property of the labels, because
the four models share training set, pipeline, loss and point subsample.

Seed disagreement. On the HiLift full split, the per-case disagreement
between a model's two seeds correlates with its per-case error at
Spearman 0.15 for MT2 and 0.19 for GeoTransolver (this analysis scores
pressure on the gauge-pressure scale ‖p̂ − p‖/‖p − p_∞‖, a different
scale from the recipe metric, on which the same checkpoints read
0.11--0.12 rather than 0.041--0.042; the rank correlations are
scale-free), against about +0.6 for
both at 210 training cases and +0.67 for MT2 at 35
(@sec-data-efficiency). At full data, where a model is uncertain is no
longer where it is wrong, and two-seed ensembling gains only 3--4%. The
same artifact shows MT2 with the larger seed-to-seed prediction spread
on both datasets, which is why the learning-rate robustness of
@sec-robustness-lr must not be read as robustness to seed.

Tokens per case. Reducing MT2 from 10,000 to 6,500 tokens per case on
DrivAerML costs 8% in pressure error (0.0684 against 0.0633 at the same
learning rate), so at 10,000 tokens the error is still resolution-bound
rather than saturated. If the shared residual is a floor, it is a floor
of the protocol (the token count, the sampled-point supervision, the
labels) and not of either architecture, and the flattening of MT2's
data-efficiency curve toward 1,260 cases (@fig-hilift-data-efficiency)
would then be the floor asserting itself rather than a property of MT2.
GeoTransolver's steeper approach to the same point cannot continue
below it either.

The direct test is to train both architectures on the 1,260-case split
at 20,000 tokens per case and ask whether the parity point moves down
together, apart, or not at all. That is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status), so the statement stands as a current
understanding supported by three consistent measurements, not as a
result.

This is also the right place to state what the parity result is and is
not. It is a two-seed, one-split measurement per dataset that MT2 and
GeoTransolver reach the same accuracy at 1,260 HiLift cases and differ
by 8.5% at 435 DrivAerML cars under a fixed protocol. It does not say
that the two architectures are equivalent, which the 2.5--2.8x gap at
35--210 cases (@sec-data-efficiency), the robustness columns of
@tbl-frontier, and the 2.6x interior gap in GeoTransolver's favour
(@sec-interior) each contradict in a different direction. The
architectures agree at full data because full data lets a flexible model
learn what a structured one was built to know, and because both then
run into the same limit; where the data is scarce or the protocol is
perturbed, they come apart, and @sec-limits collects where each one
stops.
